title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 113 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 568–571 (Night 113, continuing directly from nights-112), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 113 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. ʿAzīz goes on with his tale to Tāj al-Mulūk. Looking up, he sees the woman at a copper-latticed window; she makes him a series of silent signs with her fingers and vanishes. The kerchief she dropped smells of musk and holds a slip of love verses, with more verses worked into its borders. He comes home late at night to find the wedding guests, the judge and the witnesses gone and his father furious; his cousin and bride ʿAzīza, weeping, hears the whole story, answers it with a poem on love as compulsion, and reads the signs for him: she will meet him at the same place in two days. He waits the two days at home, his head in ʿAzīza's lap. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the thirteenth after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and thirteenth night,
sentences.n: al-thālithata ʿashara, “thirteenth”: the print again has the masculine عشر beside the feminine night, and it is vocalised as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّابَّ قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَرَفَعْتُ رَأْسِي إِلَى فَوْقُ لِأَنْظُرَ مِنْ أَيْنَ سَقَطَ هَذَا الْمِنْدِيلُ فَوَقَعَتْ عَيْنِي فِي عَيْنِ صَاحِبَةِ هَذَا الْغَزَالِ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-rafaʿtu raʾsī ilā fawqu li-anẓura min ayna saqaṭa hādhā al-mindīlu fa-waqaʿat ʿaynī fī ʿayni ṣāḥibati hādhā al-ghazāli
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the youth said to Tāj al-Mulūk: So I raised my head to above, to look from where this kerchief fell; and my eye fell in the eye of the owner (f.) of this gazelle.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the young man said to Tāj al-Mulūk, “I looked up to see where the kerchief had fallen from, and my eyes met the eyes of the woman this gazelle belongs to.
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes the night up by repeating the last sentence of the one before. li-tāji al-mulūki: li-, “to”, marking whom he speaks to. li-anẓura: li-, “to, in order to”, of purpose. ilā fawqu, “upwards”: fawqu keeps its -u when it stands alone without a following noun.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِهَا مُطِلَّةٌ مِنْ طَاقَةٍ فِي شُبَّاكٍ مِنْ نُحَاسٍ لَمْ تَرَ عَيْنِي أَجْمَلَ مِنْهَا وَبِالْجُمْلَةِ يَعْجِزُ عَنْ وَصْفِهَا لِسَانِي
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bihā muṭillatun min ṭāqatin fī shubbākin min nuḥāsin lam tara ʿaynī ajmala minhā wa-bi-al-jumlati yaʿjizu ʿan waṣfihā lisānī
sentences.l: And behold, (there was) she, looking-down from a window-opening in a lattice of copper; my eye has not seen (one) more beautiful than she, and in sum my tongue is unable to describe her.
sentences.i: And there she was, looking down from a little window in a copper lattice. My eyes have never seen anyone more beautiful, and in short, my tongue cannot describe her.
sentences.n: wa-idhā bihā: idhā of surprise, “and behold”, with bi- marking who appears; it does not mean “with” here. muṭillatun, “looking down over”, from aṭalla. ṭāqa is a small window or opening in a wall; shubbāk, a lattice or grille. wa-bi-al-jumlati, “in sum”: bi-, “in”, with jumla, “the whole”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي نَظَرْتُ إِلَيْهَا فَوَضَعَتْ إِصْبَعَهَا فِي فَمِهَا ثُمَّ أَخَذَتْ إِصْبَعَهَا الْوُسْطَانِيَّ وَأَلْصَقَتْهَا بِإِصْبَعِهَا الشَّاهِدِ وَوَضَعَتْهُمَا عَلَى صَدْرِهَا بَيْنَ نَهْدَيْهَا ثُمَّ أَدْخَلَتْ رَأْسَهَا مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ وَسَدَّتْ بَابَ الطَّاقَةِ وَانْصَرَفَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾatnī naẓartu ilayhā fa-waḍaʿat iṣbaʿahā fī famihā thumma akhadhat iṣbaʿahā al-wusṭāniyya wa-alṣaqathā bi-iṣbaʿihā al-shāhidi wa-waḍaʿathumā ʿalā ṣadrihā bayna nahdayhā thumma adkhalat raʾsahā mina al-ṭāqati wa-saddat bāba al-ṭāqati wa-inṣarafat
sentences.l: So when she saw me — I looked at her — she put her finger in her mouth, then took her middle finger and stuck-it to her witness finger, and put the two on her breast between her two breasts; then she drew-in her head from the window and closed the door of the window and went-away.
sentences.i: When she saw me looking at her, she put her finger in her mouth; then she took her middle finger, pressed it against her forefinger, and laid the two on her breast between her breasts. Then she drew her head back in from the window, shut its shutter and was gone.
sentences.n: naẓartu ilayhā, “I looked at her”, stands loosely between the two clauses, with no “and” or “while”, as speech does, and is not the main verb: when she saw me, as I looked at her. al-wusṭānī, “the middle one”, is a spoken form beside Classical al-wusṭā; the print gives it a masculine ending, and al-shāhid, “the witness”, is the forefinger, raised in bearing witness to the faith. bi-iṣbaʿihā: bi-, “to”, after alṣaqa, “stick, press against”. The signs are read out by his cousin later this night.

sentences.t: فَانْطَلَقَتْ فِي قَلْبِي النَّارُ وَزَادَ بِهِ الِاسْتِعَارُ وَأَعْقَبَتْنِي النَّظْرَةُ أَلْفَ حَسْرَةٍ وَتَحَيَّرْتُ فَلَمْ أَسْمَعْ مَا قَالَتْ وَلَمْ أَفْهَمْ مَا بِهِ أَشَارَتْ
sentences.tr: fa-inṭalaqat fī qalbī al-nāru wa-zāda bihi al-istiʿāru wa-aʿqabatnī al-naẓratu alfa ḥasratin wa-taḥayyartu fa-lam asmaʿ mā qālat wa-lam afham mā bihi ashārat
sentences.l: And the fire was let-loose in my heart, and the blazing increased in it, and the glance left-me-after-it a thousand sighs-of-regret; and I was bewildered, and I did not hear what she said, and did not understand what she signalled with.
sentences.i: Fire broke out in my heart and blazed higher; that one glance left me a thousand regrets. I was bewildered: I had not heard what she said, nor understood what her signs meant.
sentences.n: Rhymed prose: al-nār, al-istiʿār. zāda bihi: bi-, “in”, the fire raging in the heart. mā bihi ashārat, “what she signalled”: ashāra bi-, “point with, make a sign of”, the verb taking bi- for the thing signed; here the bi- is drawn forward with its pronoun. “What she said” is loose: she said nothing aloud, as he tells his cousin below.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى الطَّاقَةِ ثَانِيًا فَوَجَدْتُهَا مَطْبُوقَةً فَصَبَرْتُ إِلَى مَغِيبِ الشَّمْسِ فَلَمْ أَسْمَعْ حِسًّا وَلَمْ أَرَ شَخْصًا
sentences.tr: fa-naẓartu ilā al-ṭāqati thāniyan fa-wajadtuhā maṭbūqatan fa-ṣabartu ilā maghībi al-shamsi fa-lam asmaʿ ḥissan wa-lam ara shakhṣan
sentences.l: So I looked at the window a second (time), and found it shut; so I waited till the setting of the sun, and I heard no sound and saw no person.
sentences.i: I looked at the window again and found it shut. I waited until sunset, but heard no sound and saw no one.
sentences.n: maṭbūqa, “shut”, a spoken form; Classical would say muṭbaqa.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا يَئِسْتُ مِنْ رُؤْيَتِهَا قُمْتُ عَلَى حَيْلِي مِنْ مَكَانِي وَأَخَذْتُ الْمِنْدِيلَ مَعِي ثُمَّ فَتَحْتُهُ فَفَاحَتْ مِنْهُ رَأيِحَةُ الْمِسْكِ فَحَصَلَ لِي مِنْ تِلْكَ الرَّأيِحَةِ طَرَبٌ عَظِيمٌ حَتَّى صِرْتُ كَأَنَّنِي فِى الْجَنَّةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā yaʾistu min ruʾyatihā qumtu ʿalā ḥaylī min makānī wa-akhadhtu al-mindīla maʿī thumma fataḥtuhu fa-fāḥat minhu rāʾiḥatu al-miski fa-ḥaṣala lī min tilka al-rāʾiḥati ṭarabun ʿaẓīmun ḥattā ṣirtu ka-annanī fī al-jannati
sentences.l: So when I despaired of seeing her, I rose on my strength from my place and took the kerchief with me; then I opened it, and the scent of musk wafted from it, and there came-about to me from that scent a great delight, until I became as-if I (were) in Paradise.
sentences.i: When I gave up hope of seeing her, I got to my feet, left the place and took the kerchief with me. Then I opened it, and the scent of musk rose from it, and that scent filled me with such delight that I felt as if I were in Paradise.
sentences.n: qumtu ʿalā ḥaylī, “I got to my feet”, literally “I rose on my strength”, a spoken idiom. The print writes rāʾiḥa, “scent”, both times as رأيحة, with the hamza on the alif and a plain yāʾ after it, where Classical spelling has رائحة; the word is the same, and the vowels are placed to give rāʾiḥa. ka-annanī: ka-, “as”, with anna, “as if I”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَشَرْتُهُ بَيْنَ يَدَيَّ فَسَقَطَتْ مِنْهُ وَرَقَةٌ لَطِيفَةٌ فَفَتَحْتُ الْوَرَقَةَ فَرَأَيْتُهَا مُضَمَّخَةً بِالرَّوَائِحِ الزَّكِيَّاتِ وَمَكْتُوبٌ فِيهَا هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتُ
sentences.tr: thumma nashartuhu bayna yadayya fa-saqaṭat minhu waraqatun laṭīfatun fa-fataḥtu al-waraqata fa-raʾaytuhā muḍammakhatan bi-al-rawāʾiḥi al-zakiyyāti wa-maktūbun fīhā hādhihi al-abyātu
sentences.l: Then I spread it out between my two hands, and there fell from it a dainty leaf; and I opened the leaf, and saw it steeped in the fragrant scents, and written in it (were) these verses:
sentences.i: Then I spread it out in front of me, and a delicate slip of paper fell from it. I unfolded it and found it steeped in sweet scents, with these verses written on it:
sentences.n: bi-al-rawāʾiḥi: bi-, “with”, after muḍammakh, “steeped, perfumed with”. wa-maktūbun fīhā hādhihi al-abyātu: the participle stands first, left masculine singular though its subject is plural — “and written in it were these verses”.

sentences.t:
بَعَثْتُ اِلَيْهِ اَشْكُوْ مِنَ الْجَوَى * بِخَطٍّ رَقِيْقٍ وَالْخُطُوْطُ فُنُوْنُ
فَقَالَ خَلِيْلِيْ مَا لِخَطِّكَ هٰكَذَا * رَقِيْقًا دَقِيْقًا لَا يَكَادُ يَبِيْنُ
فَقُلْتُ لِاَنِّيْ فِيْ نُحُوْلٍ وَدِقَّةٍ * كَذَاكَ خُطُوْطُ الْعَاشِقِيْنَ تَكُوْنُ
sentences.tr:
baʿathtu ilayhi ashkū mina al-jawā * bi-khaṭṭin raqīqin wa-al-khuṭūṭu funūnu
fa-qāla khalīlī mā li-khaṭṭika hākadhā * raqīqan daqīqan lā yakādu yabīnu
fa-qultu li-annī fī nuḥūlin wa-diqqatin * kadhāka khuṭūṭu al-ʿāshiqīna takūnu
sentences.l:
I sent to him, complaining of the passion, * in a fine hand — and hands are (many) arts.
And my friend said: What is (it) with your hand like this, * fine, thin, it hardly shows?
And I said: Because I am in wasting and thinness; * thus the hands of the lovers are.
sentences.i:
I wrote to him, complaining of my passion, * in a fine, thin hand — and hands have many arts.
My friend said, “Why is your writing so, * so fine and faint it scarcely shows at all?”
I said, “Because I am wasted, worn so thin: * that is the way a lover's writing goes.”
sentences.n: The verses are pointed in the print and copied as printed. Love poetry speaks of the beloved as “him” whoever the beloved is; the woman writes so here. khaṭṭ is both “handwriting” and “line”, and the poem plays on it: a lover's hand is thin as the lover. li-khaṭṭika: li-, in mā li-, “what is the matter with”. li-annī: li-, “because”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَعْدَ أَنْ قَرَأْتُ الْأَبْيَاتَ أَطْلَقْتُ فِي بَهْجَةِ الْمِنْدِيلِ نَظَرَ الْعَيْنِ فَرَأَيْتُ فِي إِحْدَى حَاشِيَتَيْهِ تَسْطِيرَ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma baʿda an qaraʾtu al-abyāta aṭlaqtu fī bahjati al-mindīli naẓara al-ʿayni fa-raʾaytu fī iḥdā ḥāshiyatayhi tasṭīra hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then after I had read the verses, I let-loose on the beauty of the kerchief the look of the eye, and saw on one of its two borders the lining-out of these two verses:
sentences.i: When I had read the verses, I let my eyes roam over the beauty of the kerchief, and on one of its two borders I saw these two lines worked:
sentences.n: tasṭīr, literally “setting in lines”: the verses are embroidered along the hem.

sentences.t:
كَتَبَ الْعِذَارُ وَيَا لَهُ مِنْ كَاتِبٍ * سَطْرَيْنِ فِي خَدَّيْهِ بِالرَّيْحَانِ
وَاحَيْرَةَ الْقَمَرَيْنِ مِنْهُ اِذَا بَدَا * وَاِذَا انْثَنَى وَاخَجْلَةَ الْاَغْصَانِ
sentences.tr:
kataba al-ʿidhāru wa-yā lahu min kātibin * saṭrayni fī khaddayhi bi-al-rayḥāni
wā-ḥayrata al-qamarayni minhu idhā badā * wa-idhā inthanā wā-khajlata al-aghṣāni
sentences.l:
The down-of-the-cheek wrote — and O what a writer it is! — * two lines on his two cheeks in sweet-basil;
Alas the bewilderment of the two moons at him when he appears, * and when he bends, alas the shame of the branches!
sentences.i:
The down upon his cheek has written — what a scribe! — * two lines in sweet basil on his cheeks;
How the sun and moon stand baffled when he shows himself, * how the boughs are put to shame when he bends!
sentences.n: Copied as printed. al-ʿidhār is the first soft beard along a youth's cheek, pictured in Arabic verse as dark writing on a pale page and as green basil. al-qamarān, “the two moons”, means sun and moon. wā- is the cry of lament or wonder, “alas for, oh the …”. yā lahu min kātibin, “what a writer he is!”: yā of wonder; li-, “for”, marking whom the wonder is about (lahu, “for him”); and min naming what kind of wonder. bi-al-rayḥāni: bi-, “with”, the ink he writes in.

sentences.t: وَمُسَطَّرٌ فِى الْحَاشِيَةِ الْأُخْرَى هَذَانِ الْبَيْتَانِ
sentences.tr: wa-musaṭṭarun fī al-ḥāshiyati al-ukhrā hādhāni al-baytāni
sentences.l: And lined-out on the other border (were) these two verses:
sentences.i: And on the other border these two were worked:
sentences.n: musaṭṭarun, “set in lines”, stands first, left masculine singular though its subject is dual, as maktūbun was above.

sentences.t:
كَتَبَ الْعِذَارُ بِعَنْبَرٍ فِيْ لُوْلُوءٍ * سَطْرَيْنِ مِنْ سَبَجٍ عَلَى تُفَّاحِ
اَلْقَتْلُ فِى الْحُدُقِ الْمِرَاضِ اِذَا رَنَتْ * وَالسُّكْرُ فِي الْوَجَنَاتِ لَا فِي الرَّاحِ
sentences.tr:
kataba al-ʿidhāru bi-ʿanbarin fī lūluʾin * saṭrayni min sabajin ʿalā tuffāḥi
al-qatlu fī al-ḥuduqi al-mirāḍi idhā ranat * wa-al-sukru fī al-wajanāti lā fī al-rāḥi
sentences.l:
The down-of-the-cheek wrote with ambergris on pearl * two lines of jet upon apples;
The slaying is in the sick (i.e. languid) eyes when they gaze, * and the drunkenness is in the cheeks, not in the wine.
sentences.i:
The down has written in ambergris on pearl * two lines of jet upon the apple of his cheek;
Death lies in languid eyes when they gaze, * and drunkenness in the cheeks, and not in wine.
sentences.n: Copied as printed; the print writes luʾluʾ, “pearl”, as لُوْلُوءٍ: the first hamza is softened to a long ū, and the second sits on the line after the wāw. The same image again: the dark down (ambergris, jet) on a pale face (pearl) and a rosy cheek (apple). al-ḥuduq al-mirāḍ, literally “sick eyes”, are the heavy-lidded, languorous eyes the poets prize. bi-ʿanbarin: bi-, “with”, the ink.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ مَا عَلَيٰ الْمِنْدِيلِ مِنَ الْأَشْعَارِ انْطَلَقَ فِي فُؤَادِي لَهِيبُ النَّارِ وَزَادَتْ بِي الْأَشْوَاقُ وَالْأَفْكَارُ وَأَخَذْتُ الْمِنْدِيلَ وَالْوَرَقَةَ وَأَتَيْتُ بِهِمَا إِلَى الْبَيْتِ وَأَنَا لَا أَدْرِي لِي حِيلَةً فِى الْوِصَالِ وَلَا أَسْتَطِيعُ فِى الْعِشْقِ تَفْصِيلَ الْإِ جْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytu mā ʿalā al-mindīli mina al-ashʿāri inṭalaqa fī fuʾādī lahību al-nāri wa-zādat bī al-ashwāqu wa-al-afkāru wa-akhadhtu al-mindīla wa-al-waraqata wa-ataytu bihimā ilā al-bayti wa-anā lā adrī lī ḥīlatan fī al-wiṣāli wa-lā astaṭīʿu fī al-ʿishqi tafṣīla al-ijmāli
sentences.l: So when I saw what was on the kerchief of the poems, the flame of the fire was let-loose in my heart, and the longings and the thoughts increased in me; and I took the kerchief and the leaf and came with them to the house, and I did not know for myself a way into the union, and could not, in the passion, (do) the detailing of the summary.
sentences.i: When I saw the verses on the kerchief, the flame broke out in my heart, and my longings and thoughts grew. I took the kerchief and the slip of paper and brought them home, not knowing any way to reach her, and in my passion unable to make sense of what she had only hinted.
sentences.n: The print writes ʿalā, “on”, as علي, with a dotted yāʾ; it is pointed here to read ʿalā. The last words are doubtful. The print sets الا جمال as two words; read here as one, al-ijmāl, “the summary”, so that tafṣīl al-ijmāl is “spelling out what was given only in sum”, which matches his not understanding her signs, and gives the rhyme with al-wiṣāl. The spacing is kept as printed. Rhymed prose: al-ashʿār, al-nār, al-afkār; al-wiṣāl, al-ijmāl. ataytu bihimā, “I brought them”: atā bi-, “come with, bring”.

sentences.t: فَمَا وَصَلْتُ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ إِلَّا بَعْدَ مُدَّةٍ مِنَ اللَّيْلِ فَرَأَيْتُ بِنْتَ عَمِّي جَالِسَةً تَبْكِي
sentences.tr: fa-mā waṣaltu ilā al-bayti illā baʿda muddatin mina al-layli fa-raʾaytu binta ʿammī jālisatan tabkī
sentences.l: And I did not reach the house except after a while of the night; and I saw the daughter of my uncle sitting, weeping.
sentences.i: It was well into the night before I reached home, and I found my cousin sitting there weeping.
sentences.n: bint ʿammī, “my paternal uncle's daughter”, is ʿAzīza, the cousin he was to marry that day.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْنِي مَسَحَتْ دُمُوعَهَا وَأَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيَّ وَقَلَعَتْنِي الثِّيَابَ وَسَأَلَتْنِي عَنْ سَبَبِ غِيَابِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾatnī masaḥat dumūʿahā wa-aqbalat ʿalayya wa-qalaʿatnī al-thiyāba wa-saʾalatnī ʿan sababi ghiyābī
sentences.l: So when she saw me she wiped her tears and came-forward to me and took-off-me the clothes, and asked me about the cause of my absence.
sentences.i: When she saw me she wiped away her tears, came to me, helped me out of my clothes and asked me why I had stayed away.
sentences.n: The print has وانبلت, a misprint for واقبلت, wa-aqbalat, “and she came towards”, and النياب, a misprint for الثياب, al-thiyāb, “the clothes”, both corrected here. qalaʿatnī al-thiyāba, “she took the clothes off me”, with two objects, is spoken usage; Classical Arabic would say nazaʿat ʿannī.

sentences.t: وَأَخْبَرَتْنِي أَنَّ جَمِيعَ النَّاسِ مِنْ أُمَرَاءَ وَكُبَرَاءَ وَتُجَّارٍ وَغَيْرِهِمْ قَدِ اجْتَمَعُوا فِي بَيْتِنَا وَحَضَرَ الْقَاضِي وَالشُّهُودُ وَأَكَلُوا الطَّعَامَ وَاسْتَمَرُّوا مُدَّةً جَالِسِينَ يَنْتَظِرُونَ حُضُورَكَ مِنْ أَجْلِ كَتْبِ الْكِتَابِ فَلَمَّا يَئِسُوا مِنْ حُضُورِكَ تَفَرَّقُوا وَذَهَبُوا إِلَى حَالِ سَبِيلِهِمْ
sentences.tr: wa-akhbaratnī anna jamīʿa al-nāsi min umarāʾa wa-kubarāʾa wa-tujjārin wa-ghayrihim qadi ijtamaʿū fī baytinā wa-ḥaḍara al-qāḍī wa-al-shuhūdu wa-akalū al-ṭaʿāma wa-istamarrū muddatan jālisīna yantaẓirūna ḥuḍūraka min ajli katbi al-kitābi fa-lammā yaʾisū min ḥuḍūrika tafarraqū wa-dhahabū ilā ḥāli sabīlihim
sentences.l: And she told me that all the people, of emirs and great-ones and merchants and others, had gathered in our house, and the judge and the witnesses came, and they ate the food and continued a while sitting, waiting for your coming, for the sake of the writing of the contract; so when they despaired of your coming, they dispersed and went to the state of their way.
sentences.i: She told me that everyone — emirs, grandees, merchants and the rest — had gathered at our house; the judge and the witnesses had come, they had eaten, and they sat on a long while waiting for you to come so that the contract could be written. When they gave up hope of you, they broke up and went their ways.
sentences.n: Her report slips from “she told me that …” into her own words to him, “your coming”, as storytellers' speech does. katb al-kitāb, “the writing of the contract”, is the marriage contract drawn up before the judge and witnesses. min ajli, “for the sake of”. ilā ḥāli sabīlihim, “on their way”, a set phrase.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي إِنَّ أَبَاكَ اغْتَاظَ بِسَبَبِ ذَلِكَ غَيْظًا شَدِيدًا وَحَلَفَ أَنَّهُ لَايَكْتُبُ كِتَابَنَا إِلَّا فِى السَّنَةِ الْقَابِلَةِ لِأَنَّهُ غَرِمَ فِي هَذَا الْفَرَحِ مَالًا كَثِيرًا
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī inna abāka ightāẓa bi-sababi dhālika ghayẓan shadīdan wa-ḥalafa annahu lā yaktubu kitābanā illā fī al-sanati al-qābilati li-annahu gharima fī hādhā al-faraḥi mālan kathīran
sentences.l: And she said to me: Your father grew-angry because of that with a severe anger, and swore that he will not write our contract except in the coming year, because he spent-at-a-loss on this wedding much money.
sentences.i: And she said, “Your father was furious about it, and has sworn he will not have our contract written until next year, for this wedding has cost him a great deal of money.”
sentences.n: The print sets لايكتب as one word, lā yaktubu. bi-sababi, “because of”: bi-, “by”, with sabab, “cause”. al-faraḥ, “joy”, is in spoken usage “a wedding”. gharima, “he paid out, bore the loss of”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ لِي مَا الَّذِي جَرَى لَكَ فِي هَذَا الْيَوْمِ حَتَّى تَأَخَّرْتَ إِلَى هَذَا الْوَقْتِ وَحَصَلَ مَا حَصَلَ بِسَبَبِ غِيَابِكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat lī mā alladhī jarā laka fī hādhā al-yawmi ḥattā taʾakhkharta ilā hādhā al-waqti wa-ḥaṣala mā ḥaṣala bi-sababi ghiyābika
sentences.l: Then she said to me: What is it that happened to you on this day, so that you were-late until this time, and there came-about what came-about because of your absence?
sentences.i: Then she said, “What happened to you today, that you stayed away till this hour and all this came about because you were gone?”

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا يَابِنْتَ عَمِّي لَاتَسْأَلِي عَمَّا جَرَى لِي وَذَكَرْتُ لَهَا الْمِنْدِيلَ وَأَخْبَرْتُهَا بِالْخَبَرِ مِنْ أَوَّلِهِ إِلَى آخِرِهِ فَأَخَذَتِ الْوَرَقَةَ وَالْمِنْدِيلَ وَقَرَأَتْ مَا فِيهِمَا وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهَا عَلَى خُدُودِهَا وَأَنْشَدَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā yā binta ʿammī lā tasʾalī ʿammā jarā lī wa-dhakartu lahā al-mindīla wa-akhbartuhā bi-al-khabari min awwalihi ilā ākhirihi fa-akhadhati al-waraqata wa-al-mindīla wa-qaraʾat mā fīhimā wa-jarat dumūʿuhā ʿalā khudūdihā wa-anshadat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: So I said to her: O daughter of my uncle, do not ask about what happened to me. And I mentioned to her the kerchief and told her the news from its beginning to its end; and she took the leaf and the kerchief and read what was in them, and her tears ran on her cheeks, and she recited these verses:
sentences.i: I said, “Cousin, do not ask what happened to me”; but then I told her of the kerchief, and the whole story from beginning to end. She took the slip of paper and the kerchief, read what was on them, and with tears running down her cheeks recited these verses:
sentences.n: The print runs yā and bint together (يابنت) and sets لاتسألي as one word. akhbartuhā bi-al-khabari, “I told her the story”: akhbara bi-, “inform of”, the verb taking bi- for the news.

sentences.t:
مَنْ قَالَ اَوَّلُ الْهَوَى اخْتِيَارُ * فَقُلْ كَذَبْتَ كُلُّهُ اضْطِرَارُ
وَلَيْسَ بَعْدَ الْاِضْطِرَارِ عَارُ * دَلَّتْ عَلَى صِحَّتِهِ اَخْبَارُ
مَا زُيِّفَتْ عَلَى صَحِيْحِ اَنْقَلِ
sentences.tr:
man qāla awwalu al-hawā ikhtiyāru * fa-qul kadhabta kulluhu iḍṭirāru
wa-laysa baʿda al-iḍṭirāri ʿāru * dallat ʿalā ṣiḥḥatihi akhbāru
mā zuyyifat ʿalā ṣaḥīḥi anqali
sentences.l:
Whoever said: The beginning of love is choice, * then say: You lied! All of it is compulsion,
and there is not, after compulsion, shame; * reports have pointed to its truth
that were not counterfeited against sound …
sentences.n: The poem is a stanza poem: three rhyming half-lines and a fourth line on a common rhyme in -di (al-ṭardi, waghdi below). Copied as printed. The last word, اَنْقَلِ, gives no sense and breaks that rhyme; the line very likely read ṣaḥīḥi al-naqdi, “the sound assay”, which fits zuyyifat, “were counterfeited”, a word for false coin; ṣaḥīḥi al-naqli, “sound transmission”, the term for reports whose chain is sound, is also possible, though it does not rhyme. The word stays as printed, and the translation stops short of it.

sentences.t:
فَاِنْ تَشَأْ فَقُلْ عَذَابٌ يَعْذُبُ * اَوْ ضَرَبَانٌ فِي الْحَشَى اَوْ ضَرْبُ
اَوْ نِعْمَةٌ اَوْ نِقْمَةٌ اَوْ اَرَبُ * تَأْنِسُ النَّفْسُ بِهِ اَوْ تَعْطِبُ
قَدْ جَرَتْ بَيْنَ عَكْسِهِ وَالطَّرْدِ
sentences.tr:
fa-in tashaʾ fa-qul ʿadhābun yaʿdhubu * aw ḍarabānun fī al-ḥashā aw ḍarbu
aw niʿmatun aw niqmatun aw arabu * taʾnisu al-nafsu bihi aw taʿṭibu
qad jarat bayna ʿaksihi wa-al-ṭardi
sentences.n: Copied as printed. ʿadhābun yaʿdhubu plays on two senses of one root, ʿ-dh-b: ʿadhāb, “torment”, and ʿadhuba, “be sweet”. taʾnisu is the less common by-form; the usual imperfect is taʾnasu. The last line is obscure: ṭard and ʿaks are the terms of logic for a statement and its converse, so love holds true both ways round; the feminine jarat has no clear subject.

sentences.t:
وَمَعْ ذَا اَيَّامُهُ مَوَاسِمْ * وَثَغْرُهَا عَلَى الدَّوَامِ بَاسِمْ
وَنَفَحَاتُ طِيْبِهَا مَوَاسِمْ * وَهْوَ لِكُلِّ مَا يَشِينُ حَاسِمْ
مَا حَلَّ قَطُّ قَلْبَ نَذْلٍ وَغْدِ
sentences.tr:
wa-maʿ dhā ayyāmuhu mawāsim * wa-thaghruhā ʿalā al-dawāmi bāsim
wa-nafaḥātu ṭībihā mawāsim * wa-hwa li-kulli mā yashīnu ḥāsim
mā ḥalla qaṭṭu qalba nadhlin waghdi
sentences.i:
And yet its days are festivals, * their lips forever smiling,
the breath of their fragrance a feast; * it cuts away all that brings disgrace,
and never lodged in a base and worthless heart.
sentences.n: Copied as printed, with the pausal endings the rhyme wants (mawāsim, bāsim, ḥāsim). maʿ is the short form of maʿa, “with”. The poem shifts between “its” (love's) and “their” (the feminine -hā, love's days); mawāsim, “seasons, festivals”, rhymes with itself, and the second may stand for another word. li-kulli: li-, “for”, with ḥāsim, “cutting off”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا قَالَتْ لِي فَمَا قَالَتْ لَكَ وَمَا أَشَارَتْ بِهِ إِلَيْكَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā qālat lī fa-mā qālat laka wa-mā ashārat bihi ilayka
sentences.l: Then she said to me: So what did she say to you, and what did she signal to you with?
sentences.i: Then she asked me, “What did she say to you, and what signs did she make to you?”
sentences.n: thumma innahā qālat, literally “then indeed she said”, a storyteller's way of opening a new step. ashāra bi- … ilā, “make a sign of … to”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا مَا نَطَقَتْ بِشَيْءٍ غَيْرَ أَنَّهَا وَضَعَتْ إِصْبَعَهَا فِي فَمِهَا ثُمَّ قَرَنَتْهَا بِالْإِصْبَعِ الْوُسْطَى وَجَعَلَتِ الْإِصْبَعَيْنِ عَلَى صَدْرِهَا وَأَشَارَتْ إِلَى الْأَرْضِ ثُمَّ أَدْخَلَتْ رَأْسَهَا وَأَغْلَقَتِ الطَّاقَةَ وَلَمْ أَرَهَا بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā mā naṭaqat bi-shayʾin ghayra annahā waḍaʿat iṣbaʿahā fī famihā thumma qaranathā bi-al-iṣbaʿi al-wusṭā wa-jaʿalati al-iṣbaʿayni ʿalā ṣadrihā wa-ashārat ilā al-arḍi thumma adkhalat raʾsahā wa-aghlaqati al-ṭāqata wa-lam arahā baʿda dhālika
sentences.l: So I said to her: She did not utter a thing, except that she put her finger in her mouth, then joined it to the middle finger and put the two fingers on her breast, and pointed to the ground; then she drew-in her head and shut the window, and I did not see her after that.
sentences.i: “She said nothing at all,” I told her, “but she put her finger in her mouth, then joined it to her middle finger, laid the two fingers on her breast and pointed to the ground. Then she drew her head in and shut the window, and I did not see her again.
sentences.n: naṭaqat bi-shayʾin, “she uttered anything”: naṭaqa bi-, “speak, utter”, the verb taking bi- for what is said. qaranathā bi-: bi-, “to, with”, after qarana, “join”. He now adds a sign he did not mention before: she pointed to the ground.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْ قَلْبِي مَعَهَا فَقَعَدْتُ إِلَى غِيَابِ الشَّمْسِ أَنْتَظِرُ أَنَّهَا تُطِلُّ مِنَ الطَّاقَةِ ثَانِيًا فَلَمْ تَفْعَلْ فَلَمَّا يَئِسْتُ مِنْهَا قُمْتُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ الْمَكَانِ وَجِئْتُ إِلَى بَيْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhat qalbī maʿahā fa-qaʿadtu ilā ghiyābi al-shamsi antaẓiru annahā tuṭillu mina al-ṭāqati thāniyan fa-lam tafʿal fa-lammā yaʾistu minhā qumtu min dhālika al-makāni wa-jiʾtu ilā baytī
sentences.l: And she took my heart with her; so I sat until the going-away of the sun, waiting that she would look-out from the window a second (time), and she did not do (it); so when I despaired of her, I rose from that place and came to my house.
sentences.i: She took my heart with her. I sat there till sunset, waiting for her to look out of the window again, but she did not; and when I had given up hope of her, I got up from that place and came home.
sentences.n: antaẓiru annahā tuṭillu, “I wait that she looks out”, with anna and an indicative where Classical Arabic would put an and the subjunctive.

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ قِصَّتِي وَأَشْتَهِي مِنْكِ أَنْ تُعِينِينِي عَلَى مَا بُلِيتُ بِهِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi qiṣṣatī wa-ashtahī minki an tuʿīnīnī ʿalā mā bulītu bihi
sentences.l: And this is my story, and I desire from you that you help me in what I have been afflicted with.
sentences.i: That is my story; and I would have you help me with this trouble that has come upon me.”
sentences.n: an tuʿīnīnī, “that you help me”: he speaks to her, so the verb is feminine (tuʿīnī) with -nī, “me”. bulītu bihi, “I have been afflicted with”: buliya bi-, the verb taking bi- for the affliction.

sentences.t: فَرَفَعَتْ رَأْسَهَا إِلَيَّ وَقَالَتْ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي لَوْ طَلَبْتَ عَيْنِي لَاَخْرَجْتُهَا لَكَ مِنْ جُفُونِي وَلَابُدَّأَنْ أُسَاعِدَكَ عَلَى حَاجَتِكَ وَأُسَاعِدَهَا عَلَى حَاجَتِهَا فَإِنَّهَا مُغْرَمَةٌ بِكَ كَمَا أَنَّكَ مُغْرَمٌ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-rafaʿat raʾsahā ilayya wa-qālat yā bna ʿammī law ṭalabta ʿaynī la-akhrajtuhā laka min jufūnī wa-lā budda an usāʿidaka ʿalā ḥājatika wa-usāʿidahā ʿalā ḥājatihā fa-innahā mughramatun bika kamā annaka mughramun bihā
sentences.l: So she raised her head to me and said: O son of my uncle, if you asked for my eye, I would have brought-it-out for you from my eyelids; and there is no escape (from it): I will help you to your need and help her to her need, for she is infatuated with you just as you are infatuated with her.
sentences.i: She raised her head to me and said, “Cousin, if you asked for my eye I would pluck it from its lids for you. I must and will help you to what you want, and help her to what she wants, for she is as much in love with you as you are with her.
sentences.n: This is the cousin ʿAzīza, the bride he has just abandoned, and she offers at once to help him to another woman. la-akhrajtuhā: the print itself sets a fatḥa on the alif. The print runs لابد and ان together (لابدان). mughramatun bika: bi-, “with”, after mughram, “infatuated with”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا وَمَا تَفْسِيرُ مَا أَشَارَتْ بِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā wa-mā tafsīru mā ashārat bihi
sentences.l: So I said to her: And what is the interpretation of what she signalled with?
sentences.i: “And what do her signs mean?” I asked her.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ أَمَّا وَضْعُ إِصْبَعِهَا فِي فَمِهَا فَإِنَّهُ إِشَارَةٌ إِلَى أَنَّكَ عِنْدَهَا بِمَنْزِلَةِ رُوحِهَا مِنْ جَسَدِهَا وَإِنَّمَا تَعَضُّ عَلَى وِصَالِكَ بِالنَّوَاجِذِ
sentences.tr: qālat ammā waḍʿu iṣbaʿihā fī famihā fa-innahu ishāratun ilā annaka ʿindahā bi-manzilati rūḥihā min jasadihā wa-innamā taʿaḍḍu ʿalā wiṣālika bi-al-nawājidhi
sentences.l: She said: As for the putting of her finger in her mouth, it is a sign that you are, with her, at the rank of her soul from her body, and indeed she bites on union with you with the molars.
sentences.i: She said, “Putting her finger in her mouth means that you are to her what her soul is to her body, and that she will hold on to you with her teeth.
sentences.n: bi-manzilati, “in the position of, as”: bi-, “in”, with manzila, “rank, place”. taʿaḍḍu ʿalā … bi-al-nawājidhi, “bite on … with the back teeth”, is a proverbial phrase for clinging to something with all one's strength; bi-, “with”, the teeth. wa-innamā, here “and indeed”, opens a second meaning.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا الْمِنْدِيلُ فَإِنَّهُ إِشَارَةٌ إِلَى سَلَامِ الْمُحِبِّينَ عَلَى الْمَحْبُوبِينَ وَأَمَّا الْوَرَقَةُ فَإِنَّهَا إِشَارَةٌ إِلَى أَنَّ رُوحَهَا مُتَعَلِّقَةٌ بِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā al-mindīlu fa-innahu ishāratun ilā salāmi al-muḥibbīna ʿalā al-maḥbūbīna wa-ammā al-waraqatu fa-innahā ishāratun ilā anna rūḥahā mutaʿalliqatun bika
sentences.l: And as for the kerchief, it is a sign of the greeting of the lovers to the beloved-ones; and as for the leaf, it is a sign that her soul is attached to you.
sentences.i: The kerchief is a lover's greeting to the beloved; and the slip of paper means that her soul hangs upon you.
sentences.n: mutaʿalliqatun bika: bi-, “to, on”, after mutaʿalliq, “attached to, hanging on”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا وَضْعُ إِصْبَعَيْهَا عَلَى صَدْرِهَا بَيْنَ نَهْدَيْهَا فَتَفْسِيرُهُ أَنَّهَا تَقُولُ لَكَ بَعْدَ يَوْمَيْنِ تَعَالَ هُنَا لِيَزُولَ عَنِّي بِطَلْعَتِكَ الْعَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā waḍʿu iṣbaʿayhā ʿalā ṣadrihā bayna nahdayhā fa-tafsīruhu annahā taqūlu laka baʿda yawmayni taʿāla hunā li-yazūla ʿannī bi-ṭalʿatika al-ʿanā
sentences.l: And as for the putting of her two fingers on her breast between her two breasts, its interpretation (is) that she says to you: After two days come here, that the hardship may go away from me by your appearing.
sentences.i: And her laying two fingers on her breast between her breasts means that she is saying to you, ‘In two days come here, so that the sight of you may take my pain away.’
sentences.n: Two fingers for two days; the pointing to the ground, which he mentioned only to her, says “here”. al-ʿanā, “hardship, distress”, is written without its final hamza (Classical al-ʿanāʾ) and rhymes with hunā. li-yazūla: li-, “so that”. bi-ṭalʿatika: bi-, “by, through”, with ṭalʿa, “appearance, face”.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ يَا بْنَ عَمِّي أَنَّهَالَكَ عَاشِقَةٌ وَبِكَ وَاثِقَةٌ وَهَذَا مَا عِنْدِي مِنَ التَّفْسِيرِ لِإِشَارَاتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam yā bna ʿammī annahā laka ʿāshiqatun wa-bika wāthiqatun wa-hādhā mā ʿindī mina al-tafsīri li-ishārātihā
sentences.l: And know, O son of my uncle, that she is to you a lover, and in you trusting; and this is what I have of the interpretation of her signs.
sentences.i: Know, cousin, that she loves you and trusts in you. That is how I read her signs.
sentences.n: The print runs annahā and laka together (انهالك). laka ʿāshiqatun, “in love with you”: li-, “for, with”, the object of her love put first. bika wāthiqatun: bi-, “in”, after wāthiq, “trusting in”. Rhymed prose: ʿāshiqa, wāthiqa. li-ishārātihā: li-, “of”, the thing interpreted.

sentences.t: وَلَوْكُنْتُ أَدْخُلُ وَأَخْرُجُ لَجَمَعْتُ بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهَا فِي أَسْرَعِ وَقْتٍ وَأَسْتُرُكُمَا بِذَيْلِي
sentences.tr: wa-law kuntu adkhulu wa-akhruju la-jamaʿtu baynaka wa-baynahā fī asraʿi waqtin wa-asturukumā bi-dhaylī
sentences.l: And if I were going-in and going-out, I would have brought-together between you and her in the quickest time, and I (would) cover you two with my skirt.
sentences.i: If I were free to come and go, I would bring the two of you together in no time and cover you both with the hem of my skirt.”
sentences.n: The print runs law and kuntu together (لوكنت). adkhulu wa-akhruju, “go in and out”: as an unmarried girl she is kept at home. asturukumā bi-dhaylī, “I would cover you with my skirt”: bi-, “with”; to cover someone with one's hem is to shield them and keep their secret. The verb is left in the plain present after la-jamaʿtu.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْغُلَامُ فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ ذَلِكَ مِنْهَا شَكَرْتُهَا عَلَى قَوْلِهَا وَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي أَنَا أَصْبِرُ يَوْمَيْنِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-ghulāmu fa-lammā samiʿtu dhālika minhā shakartuhā ʿalā qawlihā wa-qultu fī nafsī anā aṣbiru yawmayni
sentences.l: The youth said: So when I heard that from her, I thanked her for her saying, and said in myself: I will wait two days.
sentences.i: The young man said: When I heard this from her, I thanked her for what she had said, and told myself, “I will wait two days.”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَعَدْتُ فِى الْبَيْتِ يَوْمَيْنِ لَا أَدْخُلُ وَلَا أَخْرُجُ وَلَا آكُلُ وَلَا أَشْرَبُ وَوَضَعْتُ رَأْسِي فِى حِجْرِ بِنْتِ عَمِّي وَهِيَ تُسَلِّينِي وَتَقُولُ لِي قَوِّ عَزْمَكَ وَهِمَّتَكَ وَطَيِّبْ قَلْبَكَ وَخَاطِرَكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qaʿadtu fī al-bayti yawmayni lā adkhulu wa-lā akhruju wa-lā ākulu wa-lā ashrabu wa-waḍaʿtu raʾsī fī ḥijri binti ʿammī wa-hiya tusallīnī wa-taqūlu lī qawwi ʿazmaka wa-himmataka wa-ṭayyib qalbaka wa-khāṭiraka
sentences.l: Then I sat in the house two days, not going-in nor going-out, nor eating nor drinking, and I put my head in the lap of the daughter of my uncle, and she was consoling me and saying to me: Strengthen your resolve and your spirit, and make-good your heart and your mind.
sentences.i: Then I stayed at home for two days, neither going in nor out, neither eating nor drinking, with my head in my cousin's lap, while she comforted me, saying, “Be strong and steadfast; take heart and be of good cheer.”
sentences.n: The print writes the imperative qawwi, “strengthen”, with a shadda (قوّ). ṭayyib qalbaka wa-khāṭiraka, literally “make your heart and your mind good”, is a set phrase of comfort.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
